Mina
MY-nah
n. (Greek/Hebrew)
Greek mna, from Hebrew māneh (a fixed weight or sum); equal to 100 drachmas (approximately 100 days’ wages for a laborer); the unit of weight-and-currency used in the Parable of the Pounds (Luke 19:12-27). The KJV renders mna as pound; modern translations often use mina.

Biblical Definition

The mina (KJV pound) is the Greek unit of weight-and-currency equal to 100 drachmas, approximately 100 days’ wages for a laborer—a substantial sum, but smaller than the talent (60 minas) of the parallel parable in Matthew 25. The mina appears most significantly in the Parable of the Pounds in Luke 19:12-27, which Christ delivered as He was making His final approach to Jerusalem before His passion. A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return. And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come. Each servant received one mina (in contrast to the talents-parable of Matt 25 where the servants received different amounts according to ability). On the nobleman’s return, two servants reported their faithful work: one had gained ten minas with his one mina; another had gained five minas with his one mina; both were commended and given authority over cities corresponding to their gain. A third had hid his mina in a napkin out of fear, and his mina was taken away and given to the servant with ten. The structural lessons of the parable are several. First, equal distribution: every servant received the same one mina, against the talents-parable’s differentiated distribution—suggesting that the mina-parable focuses on faithfulness with what is commonly entrusted (the gospel, the Word, the basic resources of Christian discipleship) rather than on differentiated gifts. Second, occupy till I come: the explicit charge to put the mina to active use in the nobleman’s absence—the active stewardship of the deposit until the Master’s return. Third, proportionate reward: the servant who gained ten minas was given authority over ten cities; the one who gained five over five cities; the reward in the kingdom is proportionate to the faithfulness in the present age. Fourth, the judgment on the wicked servant: thou wicked servant, out of thine own mouth will I judge thee—his own rationalization (the master is austere, reaping what he did not sow) is turned against him; if he believed that, he should at least have put the mina in the bank for interest. Fifth, the dramatic conclusion involving the citizens who sent a message after the nobleman, we will not have this man to reign over us, and whose end is to be slain before him (v. 27)—the parable’s reckoning includes not only the servants of the household but the wider citizenry who rejected the king’s authority. The mina-parable therefore weaves together stewardship of the common deposit, proportionate reward in the kingdom, and the comprehensive accounting at the King’s return that includes both the faithful and unfaithful servants and the rebellious citizens alike.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MINA as a weight and a coin among the ancient Greeks, equal to 100 drachmas (about $16 in silver); the KJV renders the Greek mna as pound, used in the Parable of the Pounds (Luke 19:12-27), where each servant receives one mina to occupy until the Master’s return.

MINA, n. — A weight and a coin among the ancient Greeks; equal to 100 drachmas. In scripture, the KJV renders the Greek mna as pound; the unit of the Parable of the Pounds (Luke 19:12-27).

POUND, n. — 1. A standard unit of weight (16 oz avoirdupois in English). 2. In KJV scripture, the rendering of the Greek mna, the unit of the Parable of the Pounds, equal to 100 drachmas.

Key Scripture

Luke 19:13 — "And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come."

Luke 19:16-17 — "Then came the first, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds. And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities."

Luke 19:20-22 — "And another came, saying, Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin: For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man... And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant."

Luke 19:27 — "But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me."

Modern Corruption

The Parable of the Pounds is corrupted, on one side, by sentimentalized readings that have removed the judgment-on-the-wicked-servant and judgment-on-the-rebellious-citizens conclusions (treating it as a gentle stewardship lesson without its sober eschatological reckoning)—and on the other by certain post-millennial readings that have read the parable’s structural details as endorsing particular political programs of dominion, against the parable’s actual focus on faithful occupation-with-deposit until the King’s return.

expand to see more

The sentimentalized reading reduces the Parable of the Pounds to a gentle stewardship lesson, focusing on the good servants’ commendation and removing the parable’s sober conclusions: the wicked servant’s mina taken away and given to the faithful, and the rebellious citizens’ being brought hither and slain before the returning king. The parable as Christ told it has both registers—commendation and judgment. The faithful are honored proportionately; the unfaithful is exposed by his own words; the rebels are dealt with finally. To preach the parable’s commendation without its judgment-conclusion is to truncate Christ’s teaching and to present a softer Christ than the one Luke 19 actually gives. The recovery is the recovery of the whole parable: the stewardship of the deposit, the proportionate reward of the faithful, the exposure of the unfaithful, and the comprehensive reckoning at the King’s return that includes both household and citizenry.

The opposite corruption is the post-millennial-dominionist over-extension that has read the parable’s structural details (the nobleman receiving the kingdom; the servants given authority over cities; the rebellious citizens slain) as endorsing particular political programs of Christian dominion over earthly cities and nations. The parable is set in the context of Christ’s approach to Jerusalem and is partly addressed to the disciples’ misunderstanding that the kingdom of God should immediately appear (Luke 19:11). Its focus is the King’s departure to receive the kingdom, the saints’ faithful stewardship of His deposit in His absence, and the comprehensive reckoning at His return. The cities-of-reward in the parable belong to the kingdom-coming, not to a present-age political program. Recover both ends. Refuse the sentimentalized reading that removes the judgment-conclusions, and refuse the dominionist over-extension that treats the parable as endorsing present-age political programs. The biblical Parable of the Pounds calls every saint to faithful active stewardship of what the King has entrusted, with the King’s return as the day of reckoning when commendation and judgment are both dispensed.

Hebrew Roots

Greek mna (from Hebrew māneh); 100 drachmas; the unit of the Parable of the Pounds (Luke 19:12-27), in which each servant receives one mina and is charged to occupy till I come; substantial stewardship-and-judgment teaching at Christ’s approach to Jerusalem.

expand to see more

Greek mna (G3414) — mina, the Greek unit of weight-and-currency (9 NT uses, all in Luke 19).

Hebrew māneh (H4488) — a fixed weight, mina (1 Kgs 10:17; Ezra 2:69; Neh 7:71-72; Ezek 45:12).

Greek drachmē (G1406) — drachma (1/100 of a mina; Luke 15:8-9 of the lost coin).

Greek talanton (G5007) — talent (60 minas; the unit of the parallel Matthew 25 parable).
